TESTING THE GRAPH-CENTRIC ARCHITECTURE DIAGNOSIS, 2026-08-31. Anthony framed the shared-struct problem as "behaviour smearing" in a graph-centric architecture and listed four consequences. TWO ARE CONFIRMED, ONE HAS A DIFFERENT CAUSE THAN THE FRAME IMPLIES, AND THE DIFFERENCE CHANGES WHICH REMEDY WORKS.

═══ ✅ CONFIRMED — THREAD BOTTLENECKS, AND IT WAS MEASURED INDEPENDENTLY THIS MORNING ═══
His claim: "Parallel processing becomes difficult due to massive write-contention on one struct." That is precisely `fact:the-early-export-is-measured-and-a-property-only-write-is-invisible-to-the-net`, measured hours earlier without this frame in hand: one `RwLock` over the whole `DesignGraph`, and a concurrent `export_graph` serialising a state missing a concurrent write in 91 of 200 trials. The prediction and the measurement were arrived at independently and agree.

═══ ✅ CONFIRMED — GLOBAL COUPLING ═══
45 of 88 core modules add methods to the shared struct across 62 impl blocks; 56 of 64 uncovered coupling pairs have `impl DesignGraph` on both ends.

═══ 🛑 DIFFERENT CAUSE — CHANGE FRAGILITY ═══
His claim: "Altering a core node or edge property forces a recompile of all 45 modules." TRUE, AND THE GOD-STRUCT IS NOT WHY. Measured: the workspace holds exactly TWO crates, `reflow2-core` and `reflow2-mcp`, and all 88 core modules — the 45 included — live in `reflow2-core`. In Rust the CRATE is the compilation unit, so a change anywhere in `reflow2-core` recompiles all 88 modules whether or not they hang off `DesignGraph`.

⇒ SPLITTING THE STRUCT WOULD NOT FIX COMPILE FRAGILITY. SPLITTING THE CRATE WOULD. The frame bundles two remedies that address different symptoms:
    struct split  → fixes global coupling and write contention; leaves recompile scope unchanged
    crate split   → fixes recompile scope and would give the seam measurement something to measure; leaves the shared struct intact within each crate
They are independent and either can be done without the other.

⭐ AND IT EXPLAINS AN EARLIER MEASUREMENT THAT HAD NO EXPLANATION. `fact:coupling-and-contract-are-recorded-in-vocabularies-that-never-meet` found that of 64 uncovered coupling pairs, ZERO cross a crate boundary — recorded as a curiosity. With two crates for 116 modules, zero is the expected result, not a surprise. The seam frontier reads 13 of 72 partly because there are almost no crate boundaries for a seam to sit on.

═══ ⚠️ AND TWO OF THE THREE PROPOSED REMEDIES COLLIDE WITH DELIBERATE DECISIONS ═══
· ECS — "strip properties out of the graph nodes... store the actual data in separate arrays owned by individual modules". This fights `create_node`'s stated contract: "the store is a PROPERTY BAG ON PURPOSE, so a design can record what reflow2 never anticipated." That openness is what lets a USER's design carry vocabulary reflow2 does not know about, and module-owned typed arrays would require the set of properties to be known at compile time. It is a real option, but it trades away an extensibility the product depends on rather than an accident.
· OPAQUE NODE HANDLES — "give modules lightweight integer IDs (e.g. NodeId(42))". reflow2's ids are SEMANTIC STRINGS (`cmp:service`, `dec:export-once-per-pr`) and they are public surface: they appear in every tool call, in the committed export, in skills and in prose. An internal integer handle is possible, but the encapsulation he wants from it is already delivered by `GraphRead` without touching the id format.
· VISITOR / QUERY DRIVERS — the third is already the established migration path here, applied three times as free functions over `&dyn GraphRead` rather than as analyzer structs. Same pattern, different flavour.

⚠️ NOT ESTABLISHED: how long a full `reflow2-core` rebuild actually takes, or what a crate split would save. The compile-unit argument is read from Rust's model, not timed. Nobody has measured incremental build cost here, and `dec:idea-a-byte-backend-that-compiles-in-seconds` suggests compile time has been felt as a problem without being quantified.
